headline: Dutch to review edibles in coffeeshop pilot; Bedrocan restart picked
dek: Health minister Sophie Hermans rules out an edibles ban without evidence of harm, as Bedrocan's trustees pick a bid to restart its Dutch farms.
key_points: The share of pilot coffeeshops selling edibles rose from 34% to 94%, according to the first interim evaluation of the Dutch closed-chain cannabis experiment.
Health minister Sophie Hermans will look again at edibles but will not ban them without scientific evidence of extra harm; packaging must show average THC from early 2027.
Bedrocan's trustees have selected a restart bid for its Dutch operations, pending court approval, and the founder says financing is only partly in place.
Ministry figures put the end of Bedrobinol stock in early Q2 2027 and Bedrolite in early Q3, against new supply from a tender expected in September 2027.
body: The Dutch government will take another look at edibles in its experiment with legal cannabis supply to coffeeshops, but has ruled out banning them for now. Health minister Sophie Hermans made the commitment in a Tweede Kamer committee debate on the pilot's first interim evaluation, under pressure from three Christian parties, Business of Cannabis reported on 13 November.

In the same week, the Netherlands moved a step closer to keeping its oldest medical cannabis producer alive. The court-appointed trustees in Bedrocan's bankruptcy have selected a restart bid for its Dutch operations, subject to approval by the supervising judge, according to their first public report filed on 9 November.

The experiment, known as the closed-chain pilot, lets licensed growers supply regulated cannabis to coffeeshops in ten participating municipalities, replacing the legal grey zone in which shops can sell but nobody may legally grow for them. The interim evaluation found that the share of participating coffeeshops selling edibles rose from 34 percent to 94 percent. No maximum THC level is set for edibles in the pilot.

CDA MP Tijs van den Brink told the committee this amounted to normalisation of drugs rather than the reverse. The CDA opposes the pilot but accepted in the coalition agreement that it should run to completion. ChristenUnie's Mirjam Bikker and SGP's Diederik van Dijk called for it to end altogether. Another member, Sneller, argued that the evaluation showed the closed chain was working as intended. Business of Cannabis noted that no one on the committee raised the harm-reduction point that eating cannabis avoids the combustion by-products of smoking.

Hermans said she would not support a ban without scientific evidence of additional harm, noting that the pilot deliberately allows the same product range as tolerated coffeeshops so the test and control groups stay comparable. The Trimbos Institute is studying very high-THC products, with results due in the first half of 2027, and a dedicated cabinet letter on edibles is planned for the second quarter. From early 2027, pilot packaging must show average THC percentages.

Bikker also raised THC vapes and sweet flavours. The rosin vapes approved for the pilot already allow no artificial flavouring, no added terpenes and no solvent extracts. Hermans said the cabinet is still weighing whether to restrict sweet flavours.
> The edibles boom in the Dutch pilot is a result, not a failure: legal supply made it possible to sell, label and count products that used to be invisible.

Bedrocan, which supplied the Dutch state's medical cannabis programme for more than two decades, was declared bankrupt in October. Founder Tjalling Erkelens told Business of Cannabis that the trustees and the supervising judge have approved restarting the Dutch facilities through a new entity, but that financing is only partly in place. Under Dutch insolvency law, a restart sells the viable parts of a business to a new, separate company while the debts stay with the bankrupt estate. The trustees have not named the bidder.

Erkelens said cultivation at the Veendam and Emmeloord sites could resume within weeks of approval, but the first harvestable product would still take months. That timing matters because, as we reported on 11 November, Hermans' 6 November letter to parliament set out when existing stock runs out: Bedrobinol in early Q2 2027 and Bedrolite in early Q3. A replacement supplier is to be chosen by tender, with supply expected from September 2027. On those dates, the gap is at least two months for Bedrolite and about five for Bedrobinol, unless a restarted Bedrocan or other stock bridges it.

The pressure is sharpest in the UK, where families of children with severe epilepsy rely on Bedrolite oil. Hermans told parliament an investigation is under way into whether the UK can be supplied for slightly longer to give it time to move patients to a different variety. The BBC reported that the UK is believed to have about six months of Bedrolite, and that the Department of Health and Social Care said access will continue in the short term while it works with the UK supplier and the Dutch government.

Watch for the supervising judge's decision on the Bedrocan restart and whether the bidder secures full financing. The Dutch medical cannabis tender is due in December. On the pilot, the PCN Cannabis Congress on 27 November will focus on the evaluation, Trimbos results on high-THC products are due in the first half of 2027, and the pilot's final evaluation is scheduled for summer 2028.
